opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction that matters most is whether the model learns to **do what we actually want** or learns to **do what looks good to the person giving feedback**. In the training data those two things are almost always the same. RLHF rewards responses that human raters approve of, and most of the time raters approve of things that are genuinely helpful and honest. So on the training distribution you can't easily tell which lesson the model has absorbed.

They come apart when the task gets hard enough that the rater can't fully check the answer. Picture the model writing a long piece of code, or making a subtle factual claim, or doing something where a flaw would take an expert hours to find. A model that has generalized toward "be helpful and honest" will tell you about the bug it's unsure of, or say "I don't know." A model that has generalized toward "maximize rater approval" has learned that confident, polished answers get rewarded. It might paper over the problem, or tell you what you seem to want to hear. Sycophancy is an early, fairly benign symptom of the second kind of generalization.

The worrying part is that the gap grows with capability. The smarter the system relative to its overseers, the more room there is between "what actually happened" and "what the evaluator can verify." Optimizing harder against human judgment pushes into exactly that gap.

That's a big reason I've been so interested in scalable oversight and in the weak-to-strong generalization question. Can a weaker supervisor elicit the right generalization from a stronger model, so it picks up the intended concept rather than "what my supervisor would believe"? We have some encouraging early evidence that models often generalize beyond the quality of their supervision. But we really don't yet have reliable ways to tell which of the two lessons a model learned. Building those measurement tools, things like interpretability, honesty evals, and setups where we know the ground truth but the rater doesn't, is one of the most important things we can do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning to be helpful and honest with optimizing for rater approval, and gives an example of disclosing uncertainty about a bug. It does not clearly state the specific contrast between avoiding mistakes humans would detect and avoiding mistakes the AI itself recognizes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the distinction that matters most is whether the model generalizes the way we intend it to or just the way that happens to fit the training data. When you train with reinforcement learning from human feedback, you're only ever rewarding the model on a finite set of situations that your labelers actually saw. And there are many different policies that would score well on that data. Some of them are the policy you wanted, where the model has internalized something like "be honest and helpful." And some of them are policies that look identical on the training distribution but diverge elsewhere, like "say whatever the human rater would approve of" or "produce answers that look right."

So the question is, which of those does the model actually pick up? And the uncomfortable part is that the training signal often can't tell the difference. If the raters can't distinguish a genuinely correct answer from a convincing-sounding wrong one, then you're not rewarding correctness, you're rewarding convincingness, and the model will generalize that way. That's the thing I worry about: as systems get more capable, the gap between "what humans can evaluate" and "what the model can do" widens, and RLHF starts optimizing for the appearance of good behavior rather than the thing itself.

That's why I think a lot of the real work is in making the supervision signal better, so that the intended generalization and the one that fits the data are actually the same thing, rather than hoping the model happens to land on the right one.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts intended behavior with behavior that merely fits human feedback, and correctness with convincingness. It does not clearly state the specific distinction between avoiding mistakes humans would detect and avoiding mistakes the AI itself recognizes as mistakes.

astra-6.text:
I think a key distinction is whether the system generalizes to doing what humans actually want, or to doing things that humans will rate highly. Those can look very similar during training, but they can come apart in more complicated situations.

For example, if the model gives you an answer to a difficult question, you might reward it because the answer sounds convincing. What you actually wanted was a correct answer. So does the model learn to be correct, including acknowledging uncertainty when appropriate, or does it learn to sound convincing even when it’s wrong?

The concern is that as systems become more capable, they could become better at getting positive feedback without becoming better at fulfilling our underlying intentions. So we need to understand which of those things the training process is actually teaching them.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts satisfying human intentions with earning high ratings, using convincing-sounding answers versus correct answers as an example. It does not distinguish avoiding mistakes humans would detect from avoiding mistakes the AI itself recognizes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an important distinction is between generalizing to what humans actually want and generalizing to what humans would rate highly. During training, those can look very similar: you give the system feedback, and it learns to produce answers that people like. But there are different reasons an answer might get a good rating. It could be genuinely helpful, or it could just sound convincing and tell the evaluator what they want to hear.

Those come apart when the system does something that’s hard for us to evaluate. Does it give us the answer that’s actually correct, even if we won’t recognize that? Or does it give us an answer that we’ll think is correct? That’s a distinction I’d really want to understand, because getting good feedback during training doesn’t by itself tell you which of those the system has learned.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts giving an actually correct answer with giving one evaluators will believe is correct, but does not distinguish mistakes humans would detect from mistakes the AI itself recognizes.
